sourceCurrency.scope: General principles and consistent description/reporting of thermoplastic test-specimen injection-moulding parameters; particular conditions remain material-specific.
Injection/compression mould component terminology and symbols; terminology source, not a process-setting authority.
Thermoplastic test-specimen injection-moulding practice; material specification or supplier guidance takes precedence.
Thermoplastic moulding-shrinkage test method and process-factor context; not an absolute production-part predictor.
Current plastics-moulded-part dimensional/geometrical tolerance and acceptance framework.
Engineering-thermoplastic troubleshooting examples including demoulding, draft, cooling and venting; recommendations are material/application dependent.

Documents pressure-loss testing, gate-seal study, mould temperature mapping and machine/mould capability validation as controlled process-development exercises; training outline, not a universal procedure.
Review supporting multi-variable cooling, shrinkage and warpage interactions; not a universal settings source.
Experimental study showing cooling configuration/thermal imbalance can affect cooling time and part deformation in the studied mould; numerical results are study-specific.

claims.claim: The nozzle, sprue, runner and gate form restrictions in the melt path, and pressure demand depends on geometry, flow rate, rheology and thermal condition.
claims.exclusions: No universal pressure-drop value or geometry rule.
claims.basis: Standards support controlled process parameter description and RJG identifies pressure-loss testing; a stronger primary process-engineering source is still preferred for final wording.

claims.claim: Gate design can influence filling and the extent to which post-fill pressure affects the cavity, so gate changes can alter multiple part responses at once.
claims.exclusions: Magnitude depends on material, gate and geometry.
claims.basis: Manufacturer troubleshooting and standard process framing support coupled filling/holding effects, but exact gate-function wording still needs dedicated mould-design evidence.

claims.claim: Pressure-loss diagnosis should localize where demand increases instead of assuming the smallest visible feature is the root cause.
claims.exclusions: Sensor and test methods are machine/mould specific.
claims.basis: RJG explicitly teaches pressure-loss testing, but the public outline does not specify a universal segmentation procedure.

claims.claim: Advancing melt displaces cavity air and gases; inadequate escape can contribute to filling and surface-quality problems.
claims.applicability: Injection moulds requiring gas evacuation during filling.
claims.exclusions: Does not prescribe vent dimensions.
claims.basis: Manufacturer troubleshooting links venting with demoulding/filling-related problems; broader mechanism should gain an independent mould-design source.

claims.claim: A dark or burnt-looking mark can be consistent with trapped/compressed gas but does not uniquely prove a venting fault because thermal degradation and contamination can create similar evidence.
claims.exclusions: Actual cause requires discriminating evidence.
claims.basis: BASF troubleshooting materials document multiple mechanisms for burn/black-speck/discolouration symptoms, supporting non-unique diagnosis.

claims.claim: Permanent vent modification should be governed by the mould owner/tooling authority and mould-specific limits rather than by a generic Book dimension.
claims.exclusions: Site/tooling authorization varies.
claims.basis: The terminology standard does not establish modification authority or vent design limits; a current mould-component/tooling source and site-governance rule are required.

claims.claim: Mould thermal conditions affect cooling, shrinkage and warpage, and non-uniform cooling can contribute to non-uniform part response.
claims.exclusions: Dominant mechanism depends on polymer, geometry and tool construction.
claims.basis: Standard and peer-reviewed evidence independently support cooling/thermal-condition effects on shrinkage, deformation and warpage.

claims.claim: A temperature-control-unit setpoint alone does not prove the temperature of every mould surface.
claims.exclusions: Exact offsets depend on circuits, heat load, flow and measurement method.
claims.basis: Thermal gradients and coolant configuration effects are supported, but a direct instrumentation/control source is required before making this general measurement claim verified.

claims.claim: Cooling diagnosis should use measured thermal/process evidence rather than infer circuit performance from a controller setpoint alone.
claims.exclusions: Measurement methods and safe access are site/tool specific.
claims.basis: Temperature mapping is a recognized process-development exercise, but instrument selection, locations and safe measurement procedure require stronger controlling evidence.

claims.claim: Part release is affected by geometry, draft, surface condition, cooling and polymer contraction around mould features.
claims.exclusions: No universal draft angle is asserted.
claims.basis: Manufacturer troubleshooting links draft, cooling and shrinkage with demoulding difficulty; plastics dimensional standard supports geometry/shrinkage context.

claims.claim: Drag marks, whitening, distortion or ejector witness can indicate excessive release load but are not uniquely diagnostic of one cause.
claims.exclusions: Exact symptom set varies by material and tool.
claims.basis: Manufacturer troubleshooting presents multiple demoulding mechanisms and remedies; independent corroboration is preferred before verification.

claims.section: Do not cure tooling problems blindly
claims.claim: Process changes can alter release behaviour, but persistent mechanical interference or inadequate draft should be evaluated as tooling/design conditions rather than hidden with unstable settings.
claims.exclusions: Tool modifications require authorization.
claims.basis: BASF explicitly includes draft-angle/tooling remedies alongside process remedies, supporting separation of tooling and process causes without a guaranteed diagnosis.

claims.claim: Material identity/preparation and applicable supplier or material-specification conditions should be established before process optimization.
claims.exclusions: Does not choose the setpoints for a specific production grade.
claims.basis: ASTM explicitly directs users to material specifications or suppliers for recommended moulding conditions and gives those requirements precedence.

claims.section: Record what can reproduce the state
claims.claim: A reproducible process record should identify key process conditions with consistent parameter descriptions and units.
claims.exclusions: Regulated products may require more records.
claims.basis: ISO emphasizes consistent description/reporting of main process parameters and ASTM provides moulding-practice context.

claims.claim: Cause-and-effect conclusions are weaker when the thermal or mechanical baseline is still drifting, so controlled comparisons should be made from a repeatable state.
claims.exclusions: No universal warm-up duration is asserted.
claims.basis: RJG frames robust-process development around machine/mould capability and data-driven exercises; a stronger experimental-method source is preferred for final verification.

claims.claim: A fill study is intended to observe filling behaviour while minimizing later packing influence.
claims.exclusions: Exact implementation depends on machine, mould and material.
claims.basis: RJG teaches related systematic-moulding exercises, but the public outline does not define the fill-study method sufficiently for verified instruction.

claims.claim: A meaningful fill comparison should keep material preparation and relevant thermal/process conditions controlled while changing the intended experimental factor.
claims.exclusions: Specific controls depend on the test objective.
claims.basis: Standards support reproducible specimen preparation and controlled parameter reporting, though they do not define this production fill-study protocol.

claims.claim: Part weight, fill pattern, screw position and upstream pressure can show trends but do not by themselves prove local cavity pressure or gate state.
claims.applicability: Process diagnosis without direct in-cavity sensing.
claims.exclusions: Appropriately located sensors can directly measure local variables.
claims.basis: Current review and manufacturer evidence distinguish upstream/machine signals from cavity-state sensing and adaptive inference.

claims.claim: Pressure is required to drive melt through successive flow-path restrictions, and demand varies with geometry, flow rate, rheology and thermal state.
claims.exclusions: No universal pressure-drop value.
claims.basis: Pressure-loss testing is a recognized process-development exercise and standardized process parameters include the variables governing flow demand; wording remains non-numeric.

claims.claim: A pressure-loss study can compare controlled states or appropriately located measurements to localize where pressure demand increases.
claims.exclusions: Exact segmentation and sensors depend on machine/mould configuration.
claims.basis: RJG explicitly identifies pressure-loss testing but the public outline does not define a universal protocol.

claims.section: Do not equate machine pressure with cavity pressure
claims.claim: Displayed upstream injection pressure should not be treated as identical to local cavity pressure after intervening nozzle, runner and gate restrictions.
claims.exclusions: Sensor locations and pressure conversions vary by machine.
claims.basis: Process-control literature and manufacturer systems distinguish pressure signals/locations; machine-specific sensor definitions remain necessary.

claims.claim: The ability of holding pressure to influence cavity mass/pressure diminishes when the gate/feed path solidifies sufficiently to stop effective transfer.
claims.exclusions: Valve gates and unusual feed systems may behave differently.
claims.basis: Packing/shrinkage context and gate-seal testing are supported, but a dedicated gate-solidification source is preferred.

claims.claim: Varying hold duration and observing a stable response such as part mass can be used as evidence when estimating gate-seal behaviour.
claims.applicability: Controlled trials on a specific material/gate/mould.
claims.exclusions: A mass plateau is not a universal proof for every geometry or quality characteristic.
claims.basis: RJG publicly identifies a gate-seal study to determine hold time but the available outline does not establish the detailed measurement/interpretation rule claimed here.

claims.section: Plateau is evidence, not a universal constant
claims.claim: Any experimentally determined seal behaviour is specific to the material, gate geometry and thermal/process state and should be re-evaluated when those conditions materially change.
claims.exclusions: No universal hold time is asserted.
claims.basis: Material-specific moulding conditions and process-dependent shrinkage are established; dedicated gate-seal literature is still preferred for final verification.

summary.rule: HOLD is intentional when the public evidence does not support the exact wording or procedure strongly enough. Qualified claims retain scope and exclusions.
